grammarLessons.name: Preterite vs. Imperfect — Telling Stories from the Past
The Future Tense — Plans, Goals & Dreams
Por vs. Para — Purpose, Duration & Exchange

cards.grammarNote:
**Desarrollador** is a masculine noun; the feminine form is *desarrolladora*.
**de software** is a prepositional phrase used as an adjective, meaning 'of/for software' — it never changes form.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff is a software developer who builds apps for lawyers.
cards.phrase: Jeff es un desarrollador de software que construye aplicaciones para abogados.

cards.grammarNote:
**Aplicación** is feminine (*la aplicación*), so adjectives must agree: *móvil* stays the same for masculine and feminine but the article changes.
**Móvil** means 'mobile' and follows the noun it modifies, as is typical in Spanish.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff is building a mobile app for case management.
cards.phrase: Jeff está construyendo una aplicación móvil para la gestión de casos.

cards.grammarNote:
**Escritorio** literally means 'desk' and by extension 'desktop' in computing contexts.
**Aplicación de escritorio** follows the pattern noun + *de* + noun, a very common Spanish compound construction.
cards.englishPhrase: The desktop app works better on a large monitor.
cards.phrase: La aplicación de escritorio funciona mejor en un monitor grande.

cards.grammarNote:
**Desarrollo** is a masculine noun ('development') derived from the verb *desarrollar*.
**Backend** is a loanword used unchanged in Spanish tech contexts; it follows *de* to form a prepositional adjective phrase.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff focuses on backend development and databases.
cards.phrase: Jeff se enfoca en el desarrollo de backend y bases de datos.

cards.grammarNote:
**Programar** is a regular -ar verb conjugated like *hablar*: *programo, programas, programa…*
**Código** (code/source code) is the related noun — 'escribir código' ('to write code') is also commonly heard alongside *programar*.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff codes every morning before his meetings.
cards.phrase: Jeff programa cada mañana antes de sus reuniones.

cards.grammarNote:
**Error** is a masculine noun (*el error*) used in both general and technical Spanish.
**Bug** is the English loanword widely adopted in Latin American tech culture; you will hear both terms interchangeably.
cards.englishPhrase: There is a bug in the code that causes the app to crash.
cards.phrase: Hay un error en el código que hace que la aplicación se cierre.

cards.grammarNote:
**Corregir** is an irregular -ir verb with a stem change: *corrijo, corriges, corrige…* (e → i in the yo form and subjunctive).
**Arreglar** ('to fix/repair') is an equally valid and more colloquial alternative to *corregir* in tech contexts.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff stayed late to fix a bug before the deadline.
cards.phrase: Jeff se quedó hasta tarde para corregir un error antes de la fecha límite.

cards.grammarNote:
**Desplegar** (to deploy) is an irregular -ar verb with stem change e → ie: *despliega*; it is the technical preferred term.
**Lanzar** literally means 'to launch' and is common for deploying or releasing software to production.
cards.englishPhrase: We are going to deploy the new version tomorrow.
cards.phrase: Vamos a desplegar la nueva versión mañana.

cards.grammarNote:
**Base de datos** is feminine (*la base de datos*) and does not change in the plural — context and articles clarify number.
**De datos** means 'of data'; *datos* is the plural of *dato* ('piece of data/datum').
cards.englishPhrase: The database stores all the client records.
cards.phrase: La base de datos almacena todos los registros de los clientes.

cards.grammarNote:
**API** is used as-is in Spanish; it is treated as feminine (*la API*) because *interfaz* (interface) is feminine.
**Interfaz de programación de aplicaciones** is the full Spanish expansion, though *API* is universally used in conversation.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff connected the mobile app to the API.
cards.phrase: Jeff conectó la aplicación móvil a la API.

cards.grammarNote:
**Trabajo** is a masculine noun meaning 'work' or 'job'; it is also the yo-form of *trabajar* ('I work').
**Remoto** is an adjective that follows the noun and agrees in gender: *trabajo remoto*, *reunión remota*.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff works remotely from his home in Atlanta.
cards.phrase: Jeff trabaja de forma remota desde su casa en Atlanta.

cards.grammarNote:
**Laptop** is a widely used English loanword in Latin America; it is masculine (*el laptop*).
**Portátil** is the preferred term in Spain ('portable'); both are understood throughout the Spanish-speaking world.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff carries his laptop everywhere he goes.
cards.phrase: Jeff lleva su laptop a todas partes.

cards.grammarNote:
**Videollamada** is written as one word in Spanish (unlike English 'video call') and is feminine: *la videollamada*.
**Tener una videollamada** ('to have a video call') is the natural collocation; avoid directly translating 'make a call' word-for-word.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff has a video call with a client at noon.
cards.phrase: Jeff tiene una videollamada con un cliente al mediodía.

cards.grammarNote:
**Cliente** is typically masculine (*el cliente*) but the feminine *la clienta* exists; in a business context *cliente* often covers all genders.
**Reunión con el cliente** ('meeting with the client') is a very common phrase in professional Spanish.
cards.englishPhrase: The client wants a new feature added to the app.
cards.phrase: El cliente quiere que se agregue una nueva función a la aplicación.

cards.grammarNote:
**Fecha límite** literally means 'limit date' and is widely understood; *fecha* is feminine.
**Plazo** means 'term' or 'time limit' and is also very common: *el plazo de entrega* ('delivery deadline').
cards.englishPhrase: The deadline for this project is Friday.
cards.phrase: La fecha límite para este proyecto es el viernes.

cards.grammarNote:
**Actualizar** is a regular -ar verb derived from *actual* ('current/up-to-date'); it conjugates like *hablar*.
**Actualización** is the noun form ('update/upgrade'), as in *una actualización de seguridad* ('a security update').
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff needs to update the app before the client meeting.
cards.phrase: Jeff necesita actualizar la aplicación antes de la reunión con el cliente.

cards.grammarNote:
**Función** ('function/feature') is the most common tech term for a software feature; *característica* ('characteristic') is more formal.
**Feature** (the English loanword) is also heard frequently in Latin American tech teams alongside the Spanish equivalents.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff added a new feature to the case management software.
cards.phrase: Jeff agregó una nueva función al software de gestión de casos.

cards.grammarNote:
**Proyecto** is masculine (*el proyecto*) and is a cognate — its spelling and meaning closely mirror the English 'project'.
**Trabajar en un proyecto** ('to work on a project') is the standard collocation in Spanish.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff is working on a big project this month.
cards.phrase: Jeff está trabajando en un proyecto grande este mes.

cards.grammarNote:
**Jurídico** is the adjective meaning 'legal/juridical' used in formal and professional contexts; *legal* is also used but more colloquial.
**Software** is treated as masculine in Spanish (*el software*) and does not have a widely adopted Spanish equivalent in tech discourse.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff's company builds legal software for law firms.
cards.phrase: La empresa de Jeff desarrolla software jurídico para bufetes de abogados.

cards.grammarNote:
**Gestión** is a feminine noun meaning 'management' or 'administration'; it comes from *gestionar* ('to manage/handle').
**Casos** is the plural of *caso* ('case'), used in legal, medical, and general professional contexts.
cards.englishPhrase: The software helps lawyers with case management.
cards.phrase: El software ayuda a los abogados con la gestión de casos.

cards.grammarNote:
**Contador** is masculine; the feminine form is *contadora* — both are standard throughout Latin America.
**Contable** is the preferred term in Spain; in the US Latino context and Latin America, *contador* dominates.
cards.englishPhrase: Some accountants use Jeff's software to track billable hours.
cards.phrase: Algunos contadores usan el software de Jeff para rastrear las horas facturables.

cards.grammarNote:
**Abogado** is masculine; the feminine form is *abogada*.
**Bufete** is the word for a law firm ('bufete de abogados'), while *despacho jurídico* is also used in Spain.
cards.englishPhrase: The lawyers use Jeff's app to organize their cases.
cards.phrase: Los abogados usan la aplicación de Jeff para organizar sus casos.

cards.grammarNote:
**Empresa** is feminine (*la empresa*) and is the general word for a company or business.
**Firma** is also used, especially for law firms (*firma de abogados*), but *empresa* is the default general term.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff's company is a small software startup.
cards.phrase: La empresa de Jeff es una pequeña startup de software.

cards.grammarNote:
**Compañero** is masculine; the feminine is *compañera*; both are used for colleagues.
**De trabajo** ('of work') is the prepositional phrase that specifies a workplace colleague, distinguishing from a school companion (*compañero de clase*).
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff's coworker reviewed the code before the deployment.
cards.phrase: El compañero de trabajo de Jeff revisó el código antes del despliegue.

cards.grammarNote:
**Startup** is a widely used English loanword in Spanish-speaking tech communities; it is treated as feminine (*la startup*).
**Empresa emergente** is the formal Spanish equivalent, with *emergente* meaning 'emerging'; in conversation, *startup* is almost always preferred.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff works at a startup that builds software for law firms.
cards.phrase: Jeff trabaja en una startup que desarrolla software para bufetes de abogados.

cards.grammarNote:
**Bicicleta** is feminine (*la bicicleta*) and is the standard word across all Spanish dialects; the informal shortening *bici* is also very common.
**Montar en bicicleta** or **andar en bicicleta** are both used for riding a bike; *montar* is more common in Spain, *andar* in Latin America.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff rides his bicycle on weekends along the Beltline.
cards.phrase: Jeff monta su bicicleta los fines de semana por el Beltline.

cards.grammarNote:
**Andar** here means 'to travel/go' on a vehicle; it is a regular -ar verb in most tenses but irregular in the preterite: *anduve, anduviste, anduvo…*
**En bicicleta** uses the preposition *en* to indicate the mode of transport — compare *en coche* ('by car'), *en tren* ('by train').
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff loves riding his bike along the Atlanta Beltline.
cards.phrase: A Jeff le encanta andar en bicicleta por el Beltline de Atlanta.

cards.grammarNote:
**Ciclovía** is the standard Latin American term for a dedicated bike path or greenway (*ciclovia* without accent is also used).
**Sendero** means 'trail' or 'path' in a more general sense and is commonly used for hiking or multi-use trails.
cards.englishPhrase: The bike trail along the Beltline connects different neighborhoods in Atlanta.
cards.phrase: La ciclovía del Beltline conecta diferentes barrios de Atlanta.

cards.grammarNote:
**Tenis** is masculine (*el tenis*) and is used without an article when speaking of the sport in general: *jugar tenis* or *jugar al tenis*.
**Jugar al tenis** (with *al* = *a* + *el*) is the more formal construction; both versions are correct and common.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff plays tennis with his friends on Saturday mornings.
cards.phrase: Jeff juega al tenis con sus amigos los sábados por la mañana.

cards.grammarNote:
**Raqueta** is feminine (*la raqueta*) and is used for both tennis and pickleball rackets/paddles.
**Pala** ('paddle') is sometimes preferred for pickleball specifically, but *raqueta* is widely understood for any racket sport.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff bought a new racket for the tennis tournament.
cards.phrase: Jeff compró una nueva raqueta para el torneo de tenis.

cards.grammarNote:
**Pickleball** is an English loanword used unchanged in Spanish; it is masculine (*el pickleball*).
**Jugar al pickleball** follows the same structure as other sports: *jugar al fútbol*, *jugar al tenis*.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff plays pickleball at the park near his house in Atlanta.
cards.phrase: Jeff juega al pickleball en el parque cerca de su casa en Atlanta.

cards.grammarNote:
**Fútbol** is masculine (*el fútbol*) and is called *fútbol* (soccer) everywhere in Latin America; in Spain it is also *fútbol* — the American word 'soccer' is never used.
**Jugar al fútbol** is the standard phrase; note the accent on the first syllable: *FÚT-bol*.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff plays soccer with a local league in Atlanta on Sunday evenings.
cards.phrase: Jeff juega al fútbol con una liga local en Atlanta los domingos por la tarde.

cards.grammarNote:
**Gol** is masculine (*el gol*) and is a loanword from English 'goal', now fully naturalized in Spanish.
**Meter un gol** ('to put in a goal' = to score) and **marcar un gol** are both standard; *anotar un gol* is also used.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff scored the winning goal in the last minute of the game.
cards.phrase: Jeff metió el gol de la victoria en el último minuto del partido.

cards.grammarNote:
**Campo** is used for open playing fields like soccer or football (*campo de fútbol*).
**Cancha** is preferred in Latin America for courts and smaller enclosed or hard-surface play areas like tennis, basketball, or pickleball (*cancha de tenis*).
cards.englishPhrase: The soccer field in the park is always busy on weekends.
cards.phrase: El campo de fútbol del parque siempre está ocupado los fines de semana.

cards.grammarNote:
**Bailar** is a regular -ar verb: *bailo, bailas, baila, bailamos, bailáis, bailan*.
**Me gusta bailar** ('I like to dance') uses the infinitive after *gustar*; this is the standard pattern for expressing likes with activities.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff loves to dance on Friday nights after work.
cards.phrase: A Jeff le encanta bailar los viernes por la noche después del trabajo.

cards.grammarNote:
**Clase** is feminine (*la clase*); *de baile* is the prepositional modifier meaning 'of dance/dancing'.
**Baile** as a noun means both 'dance' (the activity) and 'a dance' (a social event); context clarifies the meaning.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff takes a dance class every Thursday evening in Atlanta.
cards.phrase: Jeff toma una clase de baile todos los jueves por la tarde en Atlanta.

cards.grammarNote:
**Marcar** literally means 'to mark' and is the most common verb for scoring in soccer and other sports.
**Anotar** means 'to note/annotate' and in sports contexts means 'to score'; it is widely used in basketball and baseball commentary.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff managed to score two points in the pickleball match.
cards.phrase: Jeff logró marcar dos puntos en el partido de pickleball.

cards.grammarNote:
**Partido** is masculine (*el partido*) and is the standard word for a sports match or game in most Spanish-speaking countries.
**Juego** ('game') is used more in everyday speech, but *partido* is always preferred for a formal sporting contest.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff won the tennis match on Saturday.
cards.phrase: Jeff ganó el partido de tenis el sábado.

cards.grammarNote:
**Ganar** is a regular -ar verb meaning 'to win', 'to earn', or 'to gain'; context determines the meaning.
**Ganar un partido** ('to win a match') is the standard collocation; note that *ganar* never takes a direct preposition before its object.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff's team won the soccer game last Sunday.
cards.phrase: El equipo de Jeff ganó el partido de fútbol el domingo pasado.

cards.grammarNote:
**Perder** is an irregular -er verb with a stem change: *pierdo, pierdes, pierde* (e → ie in stressed syllables).
**Perder un partido** ('to lose a match') is the standard phrase; *perder* can also mean 'to lose' an object or 'to miss' a bus.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff's team lost the pickleball match but played well.
cards.phrase: El equipo de Jeff perdió el partido de pickleball pero jugó bien.

cards.grammarNote:
**Entrenamiento** is a masculine noun ('training session') derived from *entrenar* ('to train'); it emphasizes structured athletic preparation.
**Práctica** is feminine and can mean either 'practice' (a sports session) or 'practice' in a general skill-building sense; both words are commonly used.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff goes to soccer practice twice a week.
cards.phrase: Jeff va al entrenamiento de fútbol dos veces por semana.

cards.grammarNote:
**Rival** is the most common word for an opponent in sports; it is the same in masculine and feminine (*el rival / la rival*).
**Oponente** is a more formal or literal translation of 'opponent' and is less common in casual sports conversation.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff's opponent in the tennis match was very fast.
cards.phrase: El rival de Jeff en el partido de tenis era muy rápido.

cards.grammarNote:
**Torneo** is masculine (*el torneo*) and is a cognate — very close to the English 'tournament'.
**Participar en un torneo** ('to participate in a tournament') is the standard collocation; *competir en* ('to compete in') is also used.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff entered a pickleball tournament in Atlanta last spring.
cards.phrase: Jeff participó en un torneo de pickleball en Atlanta la primavera pasada.

cards.grammarNote:
**Calentamiento** is a masculine noun derived from *calentar* ('to heat/warm'); it refers to a physical warm-up before exercise.
**Hacer el calentamiento** ('to do the warm-up') is the standard verbal phrase; the verb *calentar* can also be used directly: *calentarse antes del partido*.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff always does a warm-up before playing tennis.
cards.phrase: Jeff siempre hace el calentamiento antes de jugar al tenis.

cards.grammarNote:
**Entrenador** is masculine; the feminine form is *entrenadora*.
**Entrenador personal** ('personal trainer') is used for fitness coaches, while *entrenador del equipo* ('team coach') refers to a sports coach.
cards.englishPhrase: The coach showed Jeff a new technique for his tennis serve.
cards.phrase: El entrenador le mostró a Jeff una nueva técnica para su saque de tenis.

cards.grammarNote:
**bajo** Short for 'bajo eléctrico'; used in casual speech.
**guitarra baja** The fuller, more literal term; common in formal or written contexts.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff plays bass guitar in his free time.
cards.phrase: Jeff toca el bajo en su tiempo libre.

cards.grammarNote:
**tocar** Used for playing instruments; never 'jugar' for instruments.
**el bajo** The definite article 'el' is typically included when naming the instrument being played.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff practices bass for an hour every evening.
cards.phrase: Jeff practica el bajo una hora cada tarde.

cards.grammarNote:
**canción** Refers to a song in general; plural is 'canciones'.
**tema** A more casual synonym meaning 'track' or 'tune', common in music contexts.
cards.englishPhrase: That song has a great bass line.
cards.phrase: Esa canción tiene una línea de bajo increíble.

cards.grammarNote:
**lista de reproducción** The standard Spanish term; used across most platforms.
**playlist** Also widely used as a loanword, especially in Latin American informal speech.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff made a playlist with EDM, K-pop, and indie tracks.
cards.phrase: Jeff hizo una lista de reproducción con música electrónica, K-pop e indie.

cards.grammarNote:
**concierto** The standard word for any live music event.
**show** Used as an informal loanword, especially for pop and rock events in Latin America.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff went to a concert in Atlanta last weekend.
cards.phrase: Jeff fue a un concierto en Atlanta el fin de semana pasado.

cards.grammarNote:
**música electrónica** The standard Spanish equivalent of 'EDM'.
**EDM** The English acronym is also used in Spanish-speaking music contexts without translation.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff loves electronic dance music for coding sessions.
cards.phrase: A Jeff le encanta la música electrónica para programar.

cards.grammarNote:
**K-pop** Used identically in Spanish; no translation needed.
**el K-pop** The masculine article 'el' is used when treating it as a noun or genre.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff listens to K-pop while working from home.
cards.phrase: Jeff escucha K-pop mientras trabaja desde casa.

cards.grammarNote:
**música indie** 'Indie' is used as a loanword adjective in Spanish without change.
**independiente** The full Spanish word for 'independent'; rarely used for the music genre.
cards.englishPhrase: Indie music is one of Jeff's favorite genres.
cards.phrase: La música indie es uno de los géneros favoritos de Jeff.

cards.grammarNote:
**auriculares** More common in Spain; used for over-ear and in-ear headphones.
**audífonos** Preferred in Latin America; can also refer to hearing aids, so context matters.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff wears headphones while coding to stay focused.
cards.phrase: Jeff usa auriculares mientras programa para concentrarse.

cards.grammarNote:
**banda** Common for rock, indie, and similar groups; also means 'gang' in other contexts.
**grupo musical** More neutral and formal; works for any type of musical ensemble.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff's favorite band is coming to Atlanta this summer.
cards.phrase: La banda favorita de Jeff viene a Atlanta este verano.

cards.grammarNote:
**festival de música** The standard compound noun in Spanish.
**festival** Can stand alone when context is clear, just as in English.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff wants to go to a music festival in Europe someday.
cards.phrase: Jeff quiere ir a un festival de música en Europa algún día.

cards.grammarNote:
**letra** Literally 'letter', but in music it means the words/lyrics of a song.
**de una canción** The prepositional phrase clarifies it refers to song lyrics, not letters of the alphabet.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff looks up the lyrics when he discovers a new K-pop song.
cards.phrase: Jeff busca la letra cuando descubre una canción nueva de K-pop.

cards.grammarNote:
**ritmo** Covers both 'rhythm' and 'beat' in Spanish; no separate word needed.
**tiempo** Technically means 'time' or 'beat' in music theory, but 'ritmo' is more natural in everyday speech.
cards.englishPhrase: That EDM track has an incredible rhythm.
cards.phrase: Ese tema de música electrónica tiene un ritmo increíble.

cards.grammarNote:
**practicar** Used for practicing skills including instruments; also works for sports.
**ensayar** More specific to rehearsing with a group or preparing a performance.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff tries to practice bass at least three times a week.
cards.phrase: Jeff intenta practicar el bajo al menos tres veces a la semana.

cards.grammarNote:
**estudio de grabación** The full compound; 'grabación' comes from 'grabar' (to record).
**estudio** Can refer to the studio alone when context is clear, similar to 'studio' in English.
cards.englishPhrase: Seth spends a lot of time in the recording studio producing music.
cards.phrase: Seth pasa mucho tiempo en el estudio de grabación produciendo música.

cards.grammarNote:
**género musical** 'Género' alone can mean gender or genre; 'musical' specifies it's about music.
**estilo** An alternative meaning 'style', sometimes used interchangeably with 'género' in casual speech.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff's three favorite music genres are EDM, K-pop, and indie.
cards.phrase: Los tres géneros musicales favoritos de Jeff son la música electrónica, el K-pop y el indie.
literal: Los tres géneros musicales favoritos de Jeff

cards.grammarNote:
**en vivo** Means 'live' in the sense of a live performance; also 'en directo' in Spain.
**en directo** More common in Spain; 'en vivo' is preferred in Latin America.
cards.englishPhrase: Atlanta has great live music almost every weekend.
cards.phrase: Atlanta tiene música en vivo increíble casi todos los fines de semana.
literal: casi todos los fines de semana

cards.grammarNote:
**músico** Used for both professional and hobbyist musicians; feminine is 'música'.
**música** Note the accent difference: 'música' (noun, music) vs 'músico/a' (musician); context prevents confusion.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff is not a professional musician, but he loves playing bass.
cards.phrase: Jeff no es músico profesional, pero le encanta tocar el bajo.

cards.grammarNote:
**cocinar** The general verb for cooking; works for any method or meal.
**hacer la comida** A common colloquial alternative meaning 'to make food/the meal'.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff loves to cook elaborate meals on the weekend.
cards.phrase: A Jeff le encanta cocinar comidas elaboradas los fines de semana.

cards.grammarNote:
**receta** Used for both cooking recipes and medical prescriptions; context clarifies which.
**receta de cocina** The full phrase 'cooking recipe' removes ambiguity when needed.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff found a new recipe to try this weekend.
cards.phrase: Jeff encontró una receta nueva para probar este fin de semana.

cards.grammarNote:
**ingredientes** Direct cognate; plural only, same as in English.
**los ingredientes** The definite article is common when referring to specific ingredients in a recipe.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff buys fresh ingredients at the farmers market on Saturdays.
cards.phrase: Jeff compra ingredientes frescos en el mercado de agricultores los sábados.

cards.grammarNote:
**cocina** Means both 'kitchen' (the room) and 'cooking' or 'cuisine'; context distinguishes them.
**la cocina** The definite article is almost always used when referring to the room.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff keeps his kitchen very organized.
cards.phrase: Jeff mantiene su cocina muy organizada.

cards.grammarNote:
**especia** Refers specifically to a spice (e.g., cumin, paprika).
**condimento** Broader term covering sauces, seasonings, and condiments.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff adds lots of spices to make his food more flavorful.
cards.phrase: Jeff añade muchas especias para darle más sabor a su comida.

cards.grammarNote:
**preparación de comidas** The standard Spanish phrase; 'meal prep' as a loanword is also understood.
**meal prep** Used as-is in many Spanish-speaking fitness and food communities.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff does meal prep on Sundays so he can eat well during the work week.
cards.phrase: Jeff hace la preparación de comidas los domingos para comer bien durante la semana laboral.

cards.grammarNote:
**horno** Refers to any oven, including microwave ovens if specified (horno de microondas).
**precalentar el horno** 'To preheat the oven' is a very common cooking phrase worth knowing.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff preheats the oven before baking chicken.
cards.phrase: Jeff precalienta el horno antes de hornear pollo.

cards.grammarNote:
**sartén** Refers to a frying pan or skillet; grammatically feminine in most dialects (la sartén).
**cacerola** A deeper pot for sauces or soups; not the same as a flat skillet.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff heats olive oil in the pan before adding garlic.
cards.phrase: Jeff calienta aceite de oliva en la sartén antes de añadir ajo.

cards.grammarNote:
**picar** Often implies chopping finely, like mincing garlic or dicing onion.
**cortar** The general verb for cutting; use 'cortar en cubos' (to dice into cubes) for precision.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff chops the vegetables before adding them to the pan.
cards.phrase: Jeff pica las verduras antes de añadirlas a la sartén.

cards.grammarNote:
**a fuego lento** Literally 'on slow fire'; the standard way to express simmering.
**hervir a fuego lento** Adding 'hervir' (to boil) specifies that the liquid is just barely boiling.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff lets the sauce simmer for thirty minutes.
cards.phrase: Jeff deja la salsa cocinar a fuego lento por treinta minutos.

cards.grammarNote:
**plato** Means 'plate' or a specific dish (e.g., plato principal = main course).
**comida** More general; can mean a meal, food in general, or lunch depending on region.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff's signature dish is a spicy pasta with roasted vegetables.
cards.phrase: El plato estrella de Jeff es una pasta picante con verduras asadas.

cards.grammarNote:
**supermercado** The standard word; shortened to 'súper' in casual speech.
**tienda de comestibles** A more literal translation sometimes seen in formal writing.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff stops at the supermarket after work to pick up fresh produce.
cards.phrase: Jeff para en el supermercado después del trabajo para comprar productos frescos.

cards.grammarNote:
**sabor** Covers both 'flavor' and 'taste'; also used metaphorically (e.g., 'tiene sabor a jazz').
**gusto** Can mean taste in a sensory sense too, but more often means preference or pleasure.
cards.englishPhrase: The spices give the dish an amazing flavor.
cards.phrase: Las especias le dan al plato un sabor increíble.

cards.grammarNote:
**hornear** Specifically means to bake in an oven; derived from 'horno'.
**cocer al horno** A fuller alternative meaning 'to cook in the oven'; used interchangeably.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff likes to bake bread on Sunday mornings.
cards.phrase: A Jeff le gusta hornear pan los domingos por la mañana.

cards.grammarNote:
**cena** The evening meal; typically eaten later in Spanish-speaking countries than in the US.
**cenar** The verb form, 'to have dinner'; 'Jeff cenó en casa' = 'Jeff had dinner at home'.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff cooks dinner from scratch most nights of the week.
cards.phrase: Jeff cocina la cena desde cero la mayoría de las noches de la semana.

cards.grammarNote:
**sobras** Always plural; literally 'what's left over' from 'sobrar' (to be left over).
**restos** Another option meaning 'remains' or 'leftovers', slightly more formal.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff eats meal prep leftovers for lunch during the week.
cards.phrase: Jeff come las sobras de la preparación de comidas durante la semana.

cards.grammarNote:
**probar** Means both 'to taste' and 'to try'; context makes the meaning clear.
**saber** Also relates to taste but expresses how something tastes: 'sabe bien' = 'it tastes good'.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff always tastes the sauce before adding more salt.
cards.phrase: Jeff siempre prueba la salsa antes de añadir más sal.

cards.grammarNote:
**delicioso** A direct cognate; used throughout the Spanish-speaking world.
**rico** Literally 'rich', but in food contexts it means 'tasty' or 'delicious'; very common in everyday speech.
cards.englishPhrase: Everything Jeff cooks is absolutely delicious.
cards.phrase: Todo lo que cocina Jeff está absolutamente delicioso.

cards.grammarNote:
**viajar** The standard verb; often followed by 'a' + destination.
**ir de viaje** An alternative meaning 'to go on a trip'; more colloquial.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff wants to travel more now that he works remotely.
cards.phrase: Jeff quiere viajar más ahora que trabaja de forma remota.

cards.grammarNote:
**viaje** General term for any trip or journey, short or long.
**excursión** Better for short day trips or outings; not for international travel.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff is planning a trip to Japan next year.
cards.phrase: Jeff está planeando un viaje a Japón el año que viene.

cards.grammarNote:
**vuelo** Refers to a flight; from 'volar' (to fly).
**volar** The verb 'to fly'; 'volar a Madrid' = 'to fly to Madrid'.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff booked a direct flight from Atlanta to Mexico City.
cards.phrase: Jeff reservó un vuelo directo de Atlanta a Ciudad de México.

cards.grammarNote:
**aeropuerto** Compound of 'aéreo' (aerial) + 'puerto' (port); same logic as 'airport'.
**terminal** The terminal or building within an airport; useful at large international airports.
cards.englishPhrase: Hartsfield-Jackson is one of the busiest airports in the world.
cards.phrase: Hartsfield-Jackson es uno de los aeropuertos más concurridos del mundo.
literal: uno de los aeropuertos más concurridos

cards.grammarNote:
**hotel** Identical in both languages; masculine noun in Spanish.
**hostal** A budget guesthouse or hostel; smaller and cheaper than a hotel.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff always checks reviews before booking a hotel.
cards.phrase: Jeff siempre revisa las reseñas antes de reservar un hotel.

cards.grammarNote:
**pasaporte** Cognate with the English word; masculine noun.
**visa** The word is the same in Spanish; feminine in most Latin American countries ('la visa').
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff always keeps his passport up to date for last-minute trips.
cards.phrase: Jeff siempre mantiene su pasaporte vigente para viajes de última hora.

cards.grammarNote:
**ciudad** Used for any city; 'pueblo' is for a smaller town or village.
**metrópolis** Used for very large cities, similar to English; more formal or journalistic.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff loves exploring a new city on foot.
cards.phrase: A Jeff le encanta explorar una ciudad nueva a pie.

cards.grammarNote:
**explorar** Direct cognate; used for exploring places, ideas, or options.
**recorrer** A common alternative meaning 'to go through' or 'to tour'; implies covering ground.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff likes to explore local neighborhoods and try street food when he travels.
cards.phrase: A Jeff le gusta explorar los barrios locales y probar la comida callejera cuando viaja.

cards.grammarNote:
**mapa** Masculine noun despite ending in -a; 'el mapa', not 'la mapa'.
**plano** Used specifically for a floor plan or city street map; more detailed than a general map.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff uses a map on his phone to navigate new cities.
cards.phrase: Jeff usa un mapa en su teléfono para moverse por ciudades nuevas.

cards.grammarNote:
**equipaje** The collective noun for luggage in general; uncountable like in English.
**maleta** A specific suitcase; you can count maletas ('dos maletas' = 'two suitcases').
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff tries to travel with only carry-on luggage to avoid check-in lines.
cards.phrase: Jeff intenta viajar solo con equipaje de mano para evitar las filas de facturación.

cards.grammarNote:
**boleto** Preferred in Latin America for transportation and event tickets.
**billete** More common in Spain for tickets; also means 'banknote' in all dialects.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff bought a concert ticket for a show next month.
cards.phrase: Jeff compró un boleto de concierto para un show el mes que viene.

cards.grammarNote:
**destino** Means both 'destination' and 'destiny' or 'fate'; a rich word.
**lugar de destino** The fuller phrase 'place of destination' removes any ambiguity.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff's dream destination is Southeast Asia.
cards.phrase: El destino soñado de Jeff es el sudeste asiático.

cards.grammarNote:
**tour** Used as a loanword; pronounced similarly to English in most Latin American countries.
**excursión** The traditional Spanish word for a tour or day trip; more formal.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff booked a food tour to try local dishes in a new city.
cards.phrase: Jeff reservó un tour gastronómico para probar platos locales en una ciudad nueva.

cards.grammarNote:
**en el extranjero** Literally 'in the foreign (place)'; the standard phrase for 'abroad'.
**extranjero** As an adjective or noun means 'foreign' or 'foreigner'; the base word here.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff hopes to work abroad for a few months as a remote developer.
cards.phrase: Jeff espera trabajar en el extranjero unos meses como desarrollador remoto.

cards.grammarNote:
**aventura** Cognate; used for travel adventures and also romantic flings — context matters.
**vivir una aventura** The phrase 'to live an adventure' is a natural way to use the word.
cards.englishPhrase: For Jeff, every trip to a new country is a great adventure.
cards.phrase: Para Jeff, cada viaje a un país nuevo es una gran aventura.

cards.grammarNote:
**reservar** The standard verb for booking hotels, flights, and restaurants.
**hacer una reserva** The noun phrase 'to make a reservation'; often used interchangeably.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff always books his hotel in advance to get a better rate.
cards.phrase: Jeff siempre reserva el hotel con anticipación para conseguir mejor precio.

cards.grammarNote:
**itinerario** Cognate; used in both travel and business scheduling contexts.
**planificación del viaje** A looser alternative meaning 'trip planning'; less formal than 'itinerario'.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff plans a detailed itinerary before every international trip.
cards.phrase: Jeff planea un itinerario detallado antes de cada viaje internacional.

cards.grammarNote:
**escala** The standard Spanish word for a layover or connecting stop.
**vuelo de conexión** The connecting flight itself; 'escala' refers to the stop, not the flight.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff had a three-hour layover in Miami on his way to Colombia.
cards.phrase: Jeff tuvo una escala de tres horas en Miami de camino a Colombia.

cards.grammarNote:
**Amigo/amiga** masculine/feminine noun for friend; use *amiga* for a female friend.
**Mi mejor amigo** means "my best friend" — *mejor* (better/best) precedes the noun.
cards.englishPhrase: Seth is my best friend.
cards.phrase: Seth es mi mejor amigo.

cards.grammarNote:
**Pasar el rato** literally means "to pass the time" and implies casual hanging out.
**Salir** means "to go out" and is used when leaving the house to hang out somewhere.
cards.englishPhrase: I love hanging out with Seth on the weekends.
cards.phrase: Me encanta pasar el rato con Seth los fines de semana.

cards.grammarNote:
**Productor** is a masculine noun; the feminine form is *productora*.
**De música** is a prepositional phrase acting as a modifier — Spanish uses *de* where English uses a compound noun.
cards.englishPhrase: My friend Seth is a music producer.
cards.phrase: Mi amigo Seth es productor de música.

cards.grammarNote:
**Bar** is a masculine noun borrowed directly from English, used across Spanish-speaking countries.
**Ir al bar** means "to go to the bar" — the contraction *al* (a + el) is required before masculine nouns.
cards.englishPhrase: We found a cool bar in Atlanta last night.
cards.phrase: Encontramos un bar muy chévere en Atlanta anoche.

cards.grammarNote:
**Película** is a feminine noun — always use *la/una película*.
**Poner una película** means "to put on a movie"; *ver una película* means "to watch a movie".
cards.englishPhrase: That movie was really good.
cards.phrase: Esa película estuvo muy buena.

cards.grammarNote:
**Documental** is a masculine noun — use *el/un documental*.
**Recomendar un documental** means "to recommend a documentary" — a useful phrase for sharing what you've watched.
cards.englishPhrase: Seth and I watched a great documentary last weekend.
cards.phrase: Seth y yo vimos un documental genial el fin de semana pasado.

cards.grammarNote:
**Ver** means "to see" or "to watch" — it is used for TV, movies, and sports.
**¿Quieres ver una película?** is the standard way to suggest watching a movie together.
cards.englishPhrase: Do you want to watch a movie tonight?
cards.phrase: ¿Quieres ver una película esta noche?

cards.grammarNote:
**Planes** is the plural of *plan* (masculine) — it behaves regularly.
**¿Tienes planes?** is the natural way to ask "do you have plans?" without a preposition.
cards.englishPhrase: What are the plans for this weekend?
cards.phrase: ¿Cuáles son los planes para este fin de semana?

cards.grammarNote:
**Salir** is irregular in the first-person present: *yo salgo* (I go out).
**Salir a** followed by a place or activity means "to go out to" — for example, *salir a comer* (to go out to eat).
cards.englishPhrase: We like to go out in Atlanta on Friday nights.
cards.phrase: Nos gusta salir en Atlanta los viernes por la noche.

cards.grammarNote:
**Fin de semana** literally means "end of the week" — *fin* (end) + *de* (of) + *semana* (week).
**El fin de semana** (singular) refers to one weekend; *los fines de semana* (plural) means "on weekends" in general.
cards.englishPhrase: I usually relax at home on the weekend.
cards.phrase: Normalmente me relajo en casa el fin de semana.

cards.grammarNote:
**Invitar a alguien** — the person invited takes the preposition *a*.
**Te invito** means "I'll treat you" or "it's on me" — a common generous use of *invitar* in Latin America.
cards.englishPhrase: I invited Seth to come to Atlanta for the weekend.
cards.phrase: Invité a Seth a venir a Atlanta el fin de semana.

cards.grammarNote:
**Ponerse al día** literally means "to put oneself up to date" — a natural idiom for catching up.
**Con alguien** follows to specify who you're catching up with: *ponerse al día con Seth*.
cards.englishPhrase: We met up for coffee to catch up.
cards.phrase: Nos encontramos para un café y ponernos al día.

cards.grammarNote:
**Pasarla bien** is an idiomatic verb phrase meaning "to have a good time" — the *la* is a fixed object pronoun.
**La pasamos bien** (we had a good time) is the common past-tense form used after an event.
cards.englishPhrase: We always have a good time when Seth comes to visit.
cards.phrase: Siempre la pasamos bien cuando Seth viene a visitar.

cards.grammarNote:
**Recomendar** is a stem-changing verb: *e → ie* in present tense (*recomiendo*, *recomiendas*…).
**Te recomiendo** means "I recommend to you" — the indirect object pronoun *te* is required.
cards.englishPhrase: Seth recommended a great documentary to me.
cards.phrase: Seth me recomendó un documental genial.

cards.grammarNote:
**Salida** comes from *salir* (to go out) — it functions as a noun meaning "outing" or "departure".
**Nocturna** is the feminine adjective for "nocturnal/nighttime" — it agrees with the feminine noun *salida*.
cards.englishPhrase: We planned a big night out in Atlanta.
cards.phrase: Planeamos una gran salida nocturna en Atlanta.

cards.grammarNote:
**Brunch** is used as a loanword in many Spanish-speaking contexts; *almuerzo tardío* is a descriptive alternative.
**El domingo** means "on Sunday" when used without a preposition — days of the week don't take *en* in Spanish.
cards.englishPhrase: We always do Sunday brunch at our favorite spot.
cards.phrase: Siempre hacemos brunch el domingo en nuestro lugar favorito.

cards.grammarNote:
**Lugar favorito** means "favorite place" — *favorito* follows the noun it modifies.
**De siempre** is a colloquial phrase meaning "the usual" or "the go-to" spot, implying regularity.
cards.englishPhrase: I have a favorite local spot on the Beltline.
cards.phrase: Tengo un lugar de siempre en el Beltline.

cards.grammarNote:
**Novia** means girlfriend or fiancée depending on context — use *mi novia* for "my girlfriend".
**Novio** is the masculine form, meaning boyfriend or fiancé.
cards.englishPhrase: My girlfriend and I went for a walk on the Beltline.
cards.phrase: Mi novia y yo fuimos a caminar por el Beltline.

cards.grammarNote:
**Relación** is a feminine noun — use *la/una relación*.
**Estar en una relación** is the standard phrase for "to be in a relationship".
cards.englishPhrase: I'm really happy in this relationship.
cards.phrase: Estoy muy feliz en esta relación.

cards.grammarNote:
**Salir con alguien** literally means "to go out with someone" — it's the standard way to say "to date" in Spanish.
**Salía con** (imperfect tense) expresses a past habitual action — "I used to date."
cards.englishPhrase: I used to date a lot before I met my girlfriend.
cards.phrase: Salía con mucha gente antes de conocer a mi novia.

cards.grammarNote:
**Estar soltero** uses *estar* (not *ser*) because being single is a changeable state, not a permanent trait.
**Estaba soltero** is the imperfect past — "I was single" — used for ongoing past states.
cards.englishPhrase: When I was single, I spent a lot of time on the Beltline.
cards.phrase: Cuando estaba soltero, pasaba mucho tiempo en el Beltline.

cards.grammarNote:
**Conocer** means "to meet" in the preterite — *conocí a alguien* (I met someone).
**The personal a** is required before the person: *conocer a alguien*, never *conocer alguien*.
cards.englishPhrase: I met someone interesting at a concert in Atlanta.
cards.phrase: Conocí a alguien interesante en un concierto en Atlanta.

cards.grammarNote:
**Primera cita** — *primera* (first) is a feminine ordinal adjective agreeing with *cita* (date/appointment).
**Cita** can mean a date, an appointment, or a quotation — context makes the meaning clear.
cards.englishPhrase: My first date was pretty nerve-wracking.
cards.phrase: Mi primera cita fue bastante nerviosa.

cards.grammarNote:
**Coquetear** is widely understood across Latin America; **ligar** is more common in Spain.
**Coqueteaba** is the imperfect past — "I used to flirt" — for describing past habits when single.
cards.englishPhrase: When I was single, I was too shy to flirt.
cards.phrase: Cuando estaba soltero, era demasiado tímido para coquetear.

cards.grammarNote:
**Crush** is used as a loanword by younger Spanish speakers; *alguien que te gusta* is the descriptive native phrase.
**Me gusta alguien** means "I like someone" romantically — *gustar* is the standard verb for attraction.
cards.englishPhrase: I had a big crush on her before I asked her out.
cards.phrase: Me gustaba mucho antes de pedirle que saliera conmigo.

cards.grammarNote:
**Enamorarse** is a reflexive verb — it always takes a reflexive pronoun: *me enamoré*, *te enamoraste*.
**Enamorarse de alguien** means "to fall in love with someone" — note the preposition *de*.
cards.englishPhrase: I fell in love with Atlanta the first time I visited.
cards.phrase: Me enamoré de Atlanta la primera vez que la visité.

cards.grammarNote:
**Recuerdo** functions as both a noun (memory/souvenir) and a verb form (*yo recuerdo* — I remember).
**Romántico** follows the noun — Spanish adjectives typically follow the noun they modify.
cards.englishPhrase: I have a lot of romantic memories from my single days in Atlanta.
cards.phrase: Tengo muchos recuerdos románticos de mis años de soltero en Atlanta.

cards.grammarNote:
**Ex** is used as a prefix or standalone noun in Spanish, just as in English — *mi ex* or *mi ex novia*.
**Era** (imperfect of *ser*) is used for past identity/labels: *era mi novia* (she was my girlfriend).
cards.englishPhrase: My ex-girlfriend also lived in Atlanta.
cards.phrase: Mi ex novia también vivía en Atlanta.

cards.grammarNote:
**Terminar** means "to end" — *terminamos* can mean "we broke up" in a relationship context.
**Romper** is more emphatic — *rompimos* implies a sharper break; both use the preterite for a completed past event.
cards.englishPhrase: We broke up after a few months.
cards.phrase: Terminamos después de unos meses.

cards.grammarNote:
**Extrañar** takes the personal *a* before a person: *extraño a mi novia* (I miss my girlfriend).
**Echar de menos** is an alternative phrase common in Spain with the same meaning.
cards.englishPhrase: I miss my girlfriend when I travel for work.
cards.phrase: Extraño a mi novia cuando viajo por trabajo.

cards.grammarNote:
**Escribirle a alguien** literally means "to write to someone" — it covers texting, messaging, and emailing.
**Le escribo** (I'm texting/writing to him/her) uses the indirect object pronoun *le* which is built into the verb phrase.
cards.englishPhrase: I text my girlfriend every day.
cards.phrase: Le escribo a mi novia todos los días.

cards.grammarNote:
**Ir a una cita** is the most common phrasing for going on a date.
**Salir en una cita** is also used — both are natural; *ir* emphasizes going somewhere, *salir* emphasizes going out.
cards.englishPhrase: We went on a date to a rooftop bar in Atlanta.
cards.phrase: Fuimos a una cita en un bar de azotea en Atlanta.

cards.grammarNote:
**Compatible** works the same in Spanish and English — it follows the noun or the verb *ser*.
**Buena química** literally means "good chemistry" — a widely used metaphor for romantic compatibility.
cards.englishPhrase: My girlfriend and I have really good chemistry.
cards.phrase: Mi novia y yo tenemos muy buena química.

cards.grammarNote:
**Estar en una relación** uses *estar* because being in a relationship is a current state, not a permanent identity.
**Estoy en una relación** (I'm in a relationship) is what you'd say to tell someone you're taken.
cards.englishPhrase: I'm in a relationship now and really happy about it.
cards.phrase: Ahora estoy en una relación y estoy muy feliz.

cards.grammarNote:
**Celoso** is the masculine adjective; the feminine form is *celosa*.
**Tener celos** means "to have jealousy/feel jealous" — in Spanish you *have* jealousy rather than *be* jealous.
cards.englishPhrase: I'm not the jealous type.
cards.phrase: No soy del tipo celoso.

cards.grammarNote:
**Compromiso** can mean commitment, engagement, or obligation depending on context.
**Comprometerse** is the reflexive verb meaning "to commit" or "to become engaged".
cards.englishPhrase: Commitment is really important in a relationship.
cards.phrase: El compromiso es muy importante en una relación.

cards.grammarNote:
**Juntos** means "together" — it agrees in gender and number: *juntas* for an all-female group.
**En pareja** means "as a couple" and is often used to describe doing activities together as a unit.
cards.englishPhrase: My girlfriend and I cook dinner together most nights.
cards.phrase: Mi novia y yo cocinamos la cena juntos casi todas las noches.

cards.grammarNote:
**Atlanta** is the same in Spanish — proper nouns for major cities are usually not translated.
**En Atlanta** means "in Atlanta" — use *en* for location inside a city.
cards.englishPhrase: I've been living in Atlanta for a few years now.
cards.phrase: Llevo unos años viviendo en Atlanta.

cards.grammarNote:
**Georgia** is the same in Spanish — the U.S. state name is not translated.
**Es de Georgia** means "is from Georgia" — use *ser de* to express origin.
cards.englishPhrase: Georgia is my home state.
cards.phrase: Georgia es mi estado natal.

cards.grammarNote:
**Barrio** is more common in Latin American Spanish; **vecindario** emphasizes the community of neighbors.
**Mi barrio** (my neighborhood) is the go-to phrase for talking about where you live locally.
cards.englishPhrase: My neighborhood in Atlanta has great restaurants.
cards.phrase: Mi barrio en Atlanta tiene restaurantes muy buenos.

cards.grammarNote:
**Apartamento** is the standard word in Latin American Spanish; *piso* is the equivalent in Spain.
**Mi apartamento** (my apartment) — the possessive replaces the article.
cards.englishPhrase: My apartment has a great view of the city.
cards.phrase: Mi apartamento tiene una vista increíble de la ciudad.

cards.grammarNote:
**El centro** or **el centro de la ciudad** both mean downtown — *centro* alone is widely understood.
**Al centro** (to downtown) uses the contraction *al* = *a* + *el*.
cards.englishPhrase: Downtown Atlanta has a lot going on.
cards.phrase: El centro de Atlanta tiene mucho que ofrecer.

cards.grammarNote:
**Tráfico** is a masculine noun — *el tráfico* (the traffic).
**Hay mucho tráfico** is the idiomatic way to say "there's a lot of traffic" — use *haber* (hay) for existence.
cards.englishPhrase: The traffic in Atlanta is terrible, but luckily I work from home.
cards.phrase: El tráfico en Atlanta es terrible, pero por suerte trabajo desde casa.

cards.grammarNote:
**Vida urbana** is a formal pairing; *vida en la ciudad* is more conversational.
**Me encanta** (I love) + noun or infinitive is a high-frequency expression of strong preference.
cards.englishPhrase: I really enjoy city life in Atlanta.
cards.phrase: Me encanta la vida urbana en Atlanta.

cards.grammarNote:
**Parque** is a masculine noun — *el parque*, *un parque*.
**Ir al parque** means "to go to the park" — the contraction *al* is used with masculine nouns.
cards.englishPhrase: There's a great park near my apartment in Atlanta.
cards.phrase: Hay un parque genial cerca de mi apartamento en Atlanta.

cards.grammarNote:
**Vivir en** is the standard phrase — *vivo en Atlanta* (I live in Atlanta).
**Llevar viviendo en** expresses duration: *llevo tres años viviendo en Atlanta* (I've been living in Atlanta for three years).
cards.englishPhrase: I've lived in Atlanta for several years.
cards.phrase: He vivido en Atlanta durante varios años.

cards.grammarNote:
**Suburbio** in Spanish can have a negative connotation (slum); *zona residencial* or *las afueras* more accurately means a residential suburb.
**Las afueras** literally means "the outskirts" and is commonly used for suburban areas.
cards.englishPhrase: I prefer the city over the suburbs.
cards.phrase: Prefiero la ciudad a las afueras.

cards.grammarNote:
**Hace calor** is the standard weather expression — literally "it makes heat." Never say *es calor* or *está calor*.
**Tengo calor** means "I'm hot" (feeling hot) — use *tener* for body sensations, *hacer* for weather.
cards.englishPhrase: It gets really hot in Atlanta in the summer.
cards.phrase: En Atlanta hace mucho calor en el verano.

cards.grammarNote:
**Húmedo** means humid or damp; **bochornoso** specifically means muggy and stifling — closer to how Atlanta summers feel.
**Está muy bochornoso** uses *estar* because humidity is a temporary weather condition.
cards.englishPhrase: Atlanta summers are incredibly hot and humid.
cards.phrase: Los veranos en Atlanta son increíblemente calurosos y húmedos.

cards.grammarNote:
**El Beltline** — the Spanish article *el* is added before the proper name, as it refers to a specific trail.
**Caminar por el Beltline** means "to walk along the Beltline" — *por* conveys movement along a path.
cards.englishPhrase: I love biking along the Beltline on Sunday mornings.
cards.phrase: Me encanta andar en bici por el Beltline los domingos por la mañana.

cards.grammarNote:
**Oficina en casa** is the most natural Spanish translation — *home office* is also widely used as a loanword.
**Trabajar desde casa** (to work from home) is the standard phrase for remote work.
cards.englishPhrase: I've set up a really comfortable home office.
cards.phrase: He armado una oficina en casa muy cómoda.

cards.grammarNote:
**Ir al centro** uses the contraction *al* (a + el) before the masculine noun *centro*.
**Bajar al centro** (to go down to downtown) is also common, reflecting the idea of heading into the city center.
cards.englishPhrase: On weekends I like to go downtown to explore.
cards.phrase: Los fines de semana me gusta ir al centro a explorar.

cards.grammarNote:
**Alquiler** is standard in most of Latin America and Spain; **renta** is commonly used in Mexico.
**Pagar el alquiler** means "to pay the rent" — note that Spanish uses the definite article where English often does not.
cards.englishPhrase: Rent in Atlanta has gotten really expensive.
cards.phrase: El alquiler en Atlanta se ha vuelto muy caro.

cards.grammarNote:
**Vivir solo** — *solo* here is an adjective meaning "alone," agreeing with the subject.
**Solo** (without accent) means "alone"; **sólo** (with accent, now optional in modern Spanish) means "only."
cards.englishPhrase: I enjoy living alone — it gives me a lot of freedom.
cards.phrase: Disfruto vivir solo, me da mucha libertad.

cards.grammarNote:
**La familia** is feminine in Spanish and uses the definite article *la*.
**Querer** (to want) is an *e→ie* stem-changing verb: *quiero, quieres, quiere*.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff wants to have a family of his own someday.
cards.phrase: Jeff quiere tener su propia familia algún día.

cards.grammarNote:
**Hijos** refers to one's own children (sons/daughters), while **niños** means children in a general sense.
**Algún día** (someday) is a common adverbial phrase used with future plans.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff wants to have kids someday.
cards.phrase: Jeff quiere tener hijos algún día.

cards.grammarNote:
**Formar** means to form or to start in this context; *formar una familia* is the standard phrase for starting a family.
**Es uno de sus sueños** (it is one of his dreams) uses **ser** because it describes a defining characteristic or identity.
cards.englishPhrase: Starting a family is one of Jeff's biggest goals.
cards.phrase: Formar una familia es uno de los grandes sueños de Jeff.

cards.grammarNote:
**Casa** generally means house or home; saying *comprar una casa* (to buy a house) implies ownership.
**Querer + infinitive** expresses desire: *quiero comprar* = I want to buy.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff wants to buy a house in Atlanta.
cards.phrase: Jeff quiere comprar una casa en Atlanta.

cards.grammarNote:
**Sueño** can mean both a sleeping dream and a life dream/aspiration; **meta** is more concrete, like a goal or target.
**Tener** (to have) is irregular in the yo form: *tengo*, and is used to express possession of goals.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff has many dreams and goals for his future.
cards.phrase: Jeff tiene muchos sueños y metas para su futuro.

cards.grammarNote:
**Futuro** is a masculine noun, so it pairs with *el* and masculine adjectives.
**Pensar en** (to think about) takes the preposition *en* before the object being thought about.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff often thinks about the future and where he wants to be.
cards.phrase: Jeff a menudo piensa en el futuro y en dónde quiere estar.

cards.grammarNote:
**Casarse** is a reflexive verb meaning to get married; the reflexive pronoun changes with the subject: *me caso, te casas, se casa*.
**Espera** here comes from **esperar** which can mean to hope or to wait; context determines the meaning.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff hopes to get married someday.
cards.phrase: Jeff espera casarse algún día.

cards.grammarNote:
**Matrimonio** refers to the institution of marriage or to a married couple; it is masculine.
**Creer en** (to believe in) requires the preposition *en* before the concept believed in.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff believes in marriage and building a life with a partner.
cards.phrase: Jeff cree en el matrimonio y en construir una vida con su pareja.

cards.grammarNote:
**Establecerse** is a reflexive verb meaning to establish oneself or settle somewhere.
**Sentar cabeza** is an idiomatic expression meaning to settle down and become more serious/stable in life.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff is thinking about settling down in Atlanta.
cards.phrase: Jeff está pensando en establecerse en Atlanta.

cards.grammarNote:
**Planear** and **planificar** are both accepted; *planear* is more common in everyday speech.
**El futuro** (the future) is used here as the direct object of the planning.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff likes to plan ahead for his future.
cards.phrase: A Jeff le gusta planear su futuro con anticipación.

cards.grammarNote:
**Bebé** is masculine in Spanish even when referring to a girl; you say *el bebé*.
**Tener un bebé** is the standard phrase for having a baby; it uses **tener** (to have).
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff would love to have a baby one day.
cards.phrase: A Jeff le encantaría tener un bebé algún día.

cards.grammarNote:
**Padre** is the formal word for father, while **papá** is the informal, affectionate term like "dad".
**Convertirse en** means to become (something); it is used for changes in role or identity.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff hopes to become a great father someday.
cards.phrase: Jeff espera convertirse en un gran padre algún día.

cards.grammarNote:
**Madre** is the formal word for mother; **mamá** is the warm, everyday equivalent of "mom".
**Enseñar** (to teach) takes an indirect object pronoun (*le*, *les*) for the person being taught.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff's mom taught him a lot about family.
cards.phrase: La mamá de Jeff le enseñó mucho sobre la familia.

cards.grammarNote:
**Criar** means to raise or bring up (children); it requires the personal *a* before *los hijos* because they are specific people.
**Bien** (well) is an adverb that modifies the verb and does not change form.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff wants to raise his children well.
cards.phrase: Jeff quiere criar bien a sus hijos.

cards.grammarNote:
**Pareja** is flexible and can mean romantic partner, couple, or pair; it is commonly used in modern speech.
**Cónyuge** is the more formal/legal term for spouse and is gender-neutral.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff's girlfriend is his partner in life.
cards.phrase: La novia de Jeff es su pareja en la vida.

cards.grammarNote:
**Ahorrar** is a regular -ar verb meaning to save (money or time); do not confuse it with *guardar* which means to keep or store.
**Para + infinitive** expresses purpose: *para comprar* = in order to buy.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff is saving money to buy a house.
cards.phrase: Jeff está ahorrando dinero para comprar una casa.

cards.grammarNote:
**Estable** is an adjective meaning stable; **estabilidad** is the noun form meaning stability.
**Llevar una vida** (to lead/live a life) is a fixed expression; *llevar* here does not mean to carry.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff wants to lead a stable life with his family.
cards.phrase: Jeff quiere llevar una vida estable con su familia.

cards.grammarNote:
**Algún día** means someday or one day (in the future); *algún* is the shortened form of *alguno* used before masculine singular nouns.
**Un día** can also mean one day but is more neutral; *algún día* carries a hopeful or aspirational tone.
cards.englishPhrase: Someday Jeff hopes to have everything he dreams of.
cards.phrase: Algún día Jeff espera tener todo lo que sueña.

cards.grammarNote:
**Leer** is a regular -er verb in most forms but has an irregular preterite: *leí, leíste, leyó, leímos, leyeron*.
**En su tiempo libre** (in his free time) is a common prepositional phrase for talking about hobbies.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff loves to read in his free time.
cards.phrase: A Jeff le encanta leer en su tiempo libre.

cards.grammarNote:
**Libro** is a masculine noun: *el libro, un libro*.
**Estar leyendo** is the present progressive, formed with *estar* + the gerund *leyendo*, used for actions happening right now.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff is reading a really good book this week.
cards.phrase: Jeff está leyendo un libro muy bueno esta semana.

cards.grammarNote:
**Novela** is a feminine noun referring to a novel (long fiction); not to be confused with *novela* in telenovela, which also derives from this word.
**Acabar de + infinitive** expresses a recently completed action: *acaba de empezar* = has just started.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff just started reading a new novel.
cards.phrase: Jeff acaba de empezar a leer una novela nueva.

cards.grammarNote:
**Capítulo** is masculine: *el capítulo*; note the written accent on the first syllable.
**Antes de + infinitive** (before doing something) is a useful structure for describing sequences: *antes de dormir* = before sleeping.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff reads at least one chapter before bed.
cards.phrase: Jeff lee al menos un capítulo antes de dormir.

cards.grammarNote:
**Dibujar** is a regular -ar verb meaning to draw or sketch; *hacer bocetos* is an alternative for to sketch.
**Cuando** (when) introduces a time clause; with the present tense it describes habitual situations.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff likes to draw when he wants to relax.
cards.phrase: A Jeff le gusta dibujar cuando quiere relajarse.

cards.grammarNote:
**Cuaderno de bocetos** literally means notebook of sketches; *cuaderno* (notebook) is masculine.
**Llevar consigo** (to carry with oneself) uses the reflexive pronoun *consigo* to mean on/with them.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff always has his sketchbook nearby.
cards.phrase: Jeff siempre tiene su cuaderno de bocetos cerca.

cards.grammarNote:
**Arte** is unusual: it is masculine in the singular (*el arte*) but feminine in the plural (*las artes*).
**Apreciar** (to appreciate) is a regular -ar verb and is used both for art appreciation and general appreciation.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff really appreciates art and creativity.
cards.phrase: Jeff aprecia mucho el arte y la creatividad.

cards.grammarNote:
**Lápiz** is masculine and has an irregular plural: *lápices* (the z changes to c before -es).
**Con** (with) is used to indicate the instrument or tool used to perform an action.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff prefers to draw with a pencil first.
cards.phrase: Jeff prefiere dibujar primero con lápiz.

cards.grammarNote:
**Pintura** refers to the art of painting or the paint itself; **cuadro** refers to a specific painting as an object.
**En la pared** (on the wall) uses the preposition *en* to indicate location on a surface.
cards.englishPhrase: There is a beautiful painting on the wall of Jeff's apartment.
cards.phrase: Hay un cuadro hermoso en la pared del apartamento de Jeff.

cards.grammarNote:
**Galería** typically refers to a commercial or smaller art gallery; **museo** is a museum, which can also feature art.
**De vez en cuando** (from time to time) is a fixed adverbial phrase expressing occasional frequency.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff visits art galleries in Atlanta from time to time.
cards.phrase: Jeff visita galerías de arte en Atlanta de vez en cuando.

cards.grammarNote:
**Favorito** is an adjective that agrees with the noun it modifies: *libro favorito* (masc.), *película favorita* (fem.).
**¿Cuál es...?** (What is...?) is used when asking someone to choose or identify from possibilities, not *¿Qué es?*
cards.englishPhrase: What is Jeff's favorite book?
cards.phrase: ¿Cuál es el libro favorito de Jeff?

cards.grammarNote:
**Recomendar** is an *e→ie* stem-changing verb: *recomiendo, recomiendas, recomienda*.
**Le** is an indirect object pronoun meaning to him/her/you; here it indicates the person being given the recommendation.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff recommended a great book to his friend.
cards.phrase: Jeff le recomendó un libro genial a su amigo.

cards.grammarNote:
**Autor** (masculine) / **autora** (feminine) — Spanish adjectives and nouns marking people change ending by gender.
**Escritor/a** (writer) is a near-synonym but *autor* emphasizes the creative ownership of the work.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff has a favorite author whose books he always reads.
cards.phrase: Jeff tiene un autor favorito cuyos libros siempre lee.

cards.grammarNote:
**Ilustración** is a feminine noun; its plural is *ilustraciones*.
**Estilo** (style) is masculine; *tener un estilo propio* means to have one's own style.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff is developing his own illustration style.
cards.phrase: Jeff está desarrollando su propio estilo de ilustración.

cards.grammarNote:
**Creatividad** is the noun (creativity); **creativo/a** is the adjective (creative), which agrees with the noun it describes.
**Ser creativo** uses **ser** (permanent trait) rather than **estar**, since creativity is a defining characteristic.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff is a very creative person.
cards.phrase: Jeff es una persona muy creativa.

cards.grammarNote:
**Me llamo** literally means I call myself; it uses the reflexive verb *llamarse* and is more colloquial.
**Mi nombre es** is a more direct translation of my name is and is slightly more formal.
cards.englishPhrase: Hi, my name is Jeff and I'm a software developer.
cards.phrase: Hola, me llamo Jeff y soy desarrollador de software.

cards.grammarNote:
**Soy** is the first-person singular of **ser**; professions follow *ser* without an article in Spanish (*soy desarrollador*, not *soy un desarrollador*).
**Desarrollador/a** (developer) can also be said as *programador/a*; both are widely understood.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff is a software developer who works remotely.
cards.phrase: Jeff es desarrollador de software y trabaja de forma remota.

cards.grammarNote:
**Presentarse** is a reflexive verb; the reflexive pronoun matches the subject: *me presento* (I introduce myself).
**En español** (in Spanish) is a prepositional phrase indicating the language being used.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff practiced introducing himself in Spanish.
cards.phrase: Jeff practicó presentarse en español.

cards.grammarNote:
**Pasatiempo** literally means time-passer; it is the standard Spanish word for hobby or pastime.
**Tener muchos pasatiempos** uses **tener** (to have) to express possession of hobbies.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff has many hobbies, like reading, drawing, and playing music.
cards.phrase: Jeff tiene muchos pasatiempos, como leer, dibujar y tocar música.

cards.grammarNote:
**Tiempo libre** literally means free time; *libre* (free) here means unoccupied, not gratis.
**En su tiempo libre** is a very common phrase used to talk about what someone does outside of work or obligations.
cards.englishPhrase: In his free time, Jeff reads books and sketches.
cards.phrase: En su tiempo libre, Jeff lee libros y hace bocetos.

cards.grammarNote:
**Pasión** is a feminine noun: *la pasión, sus pasiones*.
**La música, la programación y el deporte** — note that abstract nouns in Spanish often take the definite article.
cards.englishPhrase: Music, coding, and sports are Jeff's passions.
cards.phrase: La música, la programación y el deporte son las pasiones de Jeff.

cards.grammarNote:
**Talento** is masculine: *el talento, un talento*.
**Tener talento para** (to have a talent for) requires the preposition *para* before the skill or activity.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff has a natural talent for music.
cards.phrase: Jeff tiene un talento natural para la música.

cards.word: Ser bueno en / tener talento para
cards.grammarNote:
**Ser bueno en** (to be good at) uses *ser* because skill is treated as a defining trait; followed by *en* + noun or activity.
**Tener talento para** is an alternative that emphasizes innate talent: *tiene talento para la programación*.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff is really good at coding.
cards.phrase: Jeff es muy bueno en la programación.

cards.grammarNote:
**Rutina** is feminine: *la rutina diaria*; **diaria** (daily) is an adjective that must agree in gender and number.
**Desde casa** (from home) is a prepositional phrase; note it is *desde casa*, not *desde la casa*, in this fixed expression.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff's daily routine starts early since he works from home.
cards.phrase: La rutina diaria de Jeff empieza temprano porque trabaja desde casa.

cards.grammarNote:
**Rutina de la mañana** (morning routine) — *de la mañana* specifies the time of day using *de* + definite article.
**Antes de + infinitive** (before + verb-ing) is a key structure for sequencing actions.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff drinks coffee and checks his messages before starting work.
cards.phrase: Jeff toma café y revisa sus mensajes antes de empezar a trabajar.

cards.grammarNote:
**Relajarse** is a reflexive verb: *me relajo, te relajas, se relaja*.
**Después de + infinitive** (after + verb-ing) is the complement to *antes de* for sequencing.
cards.englishPhrase: After work, Jeff likes to relax and draw.
cards.phrase: Después del trabajo, Jeff le gusta relajarse y dibujar.

cards.grammarNote:
**Disfrutar** can be followed by *de* + noun (*disfrutar de la vida*) or directly by an infinitive (*disfrutar vivir*).
**La vida en Atlanta** (life in Atlanta) uses *en* to indicate location.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff enjoys life in Atlanta.
cards.phrase: Jeff disfruta de la vida en Atlanta.

cards.grammarNote:
**Estar feliz** describes a current emotional state (feeling happy right now); **ser feliz** describes a general tendency to be a happy person.
**Con su vida** (with his life) uses *con* to indicate what the happiness relates to.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff is happy with his life and where he is headed.
cards.phrase: Jeff está feliz con su vida y con el camino que lleva.

cards.grammarNote:
**Estar ocupado** uses **estar** because busyness is a temporary state, not a permanent trait.
**Entre el trabajo y los pasatiempos** (between work and hobbies) uses *entre* to link two things.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff is usually busy between work and his hobbies.
cards.phrase: Jeff suele estar ocupado entre el trabajo y sus pasatiempos.

cards.grammarNote:
**Divertirse** is a reflexive *e→ie* stem-changing verb: *me divierto, te diviertes, se divierte*.
**Los fines de semana** (on weekends) is a common time expression; note the plural with the definite article.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff always has fun on the weekends.
cards.phrase: Jeff siempre se divierte los fines de semana.

cards.grammarNote:
**Tener ganas de + infinitive** is the standard way to express looking forward to something or being eager to do something.
**El viaje** (the trip) is masculine; *tener ganas de hacer un viaje* = to look forward to taking a trip.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff is looking forward to his next trip.
cards.phrase: Jeff tiene muchas ganas de hacer su próximo viaje.

cards.grammarNote:
**Aprender** is a regular -er verb; *aprender a + infinitive* means to learn to do something.
**Cada día** (every day) indicates daily frequency; it can also be written *todos los días*.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff is learning Spanish a little bit every day.
cards.phrase: Jeff está aprendiendo español un poco cada día.

cards.grammarNote:
**Retarse** and **desafiarse** are reflexive verbs meaning to challenge oneself; *retar* is slightly more colloquial.
**Siempre** (always) is placed directly before the verb it modifies or after the auxiliary verb.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff always tries to challenge himself and keep growing.
cards.phrase: Jeff siempre intenta retarse y seguir creciendo.

cards.grammarNote:
**Mejorar** is a regular -ar verb meaning to improve or get better; it can be used transitively (*mejorar algo* = to improve something) or intransitively (*mejorar* = to improve oneself).
**En el bajo** (on the bass guitar) uses *en* to indicate the instrument or area of improvement.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff wants to improve at bass guitar this year.
cards.phrase: Jeff quiere mejorar en el bajo este año.

cards.word: Equilibrio entre trabajo y vida personal
cards.grammarNote:
**Equilibrio** (balance/equilibrium) is masculine: *el equilibrio*.
**Mantener** (to maintain/keep) is irregular in the yo form: *mantengo*; it follows the pattern of *tener*.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff tries to maintain a good work-life balance working remotely.
cards.phrase: Jeff intenta mantener un buen equilibrio entre trabajo y vida personal trabajando de forma remota.

cards.grammarNote:
**Estar orgulloso** uses **estar** because pride is an emotional state that can change; it's not a permanent trait.
**De lo que ha logrado** (of what he has achieved) uses the present perfect *ha logrado* (he has achieved).
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff is proud of what he has built in his career.
cards.phrase: Jeff está orgulloso de lo que ha construido en su carrera.

cards.english: To live fully / make the most of life
cards.grammarNote:
**Aprovechar** means to take advantage of or to make the most of; *aprovechar la vida* is a common idiomatic phrase.
**Al máximo** (to the fullest/to the max) is an adverbial phrase that intensifies the verb.
cards.englishPhrase: Jeff wants to make the most of life and enjoy every moment.
cards.phrase: Jeff quiere aprovechar la vida al máximo y disfrutar cada momento.
literal: to make the most of life
